analysis.body:
The Census BTOS measure for health care and social assistance (NAICS 62) puts AI use at 24.7% in the latest period, up from 24.0% in the prior period. The figure is the share of firms answering yes to whether they used AI in the last two weeks. That is the only adoption statistic in the source material, and it shows a sector where roughly a quarter of firms report recent AI use, with only a small change between periods.

Per WHO, AI in health holds promise for diagnosis, treatment, health research and drug development, and for supporting public health functions including surveillance and outbreak response. Per NIH, the agency makes biomedical data, including electronic health record data, omics data, imaging data, and disease-specific data, findable, accessible, interoperable, and reusable, and seeks to make those data usable with AI and machine learning applications. NIH also points to policies, guidelines, and best practices for AI in biomedical and behavioral research.

Benchmarks give a public yardstick for clinical model quality. OpenAI's HealthBench was built with 262 physicians who have practiced in 60 countries and includes 5,000 realistic health conversations with 48,562 unique rubric criteria. The benchmark evaluates diagnostic reasoning and safety. OpenAI reports that o3 outperforms Claude 3.7 Sonnet and Gemini 2.5 Pro (Mar 2025), that its frontier models improved by 28% on HealthBench, and that GPT-4.1 nano outperforms August 2024's GPT-4o despite being 25x cheaper. Artificial Analysis provides independent benchmarks across quality, price, output speed, and latency, including healthcare and medical reasoning, and lists API providers including Amazon, Azure, Google Vertex, Groq, and Together AI. The Medical Models catalog on this site tracks the 1,000 most-downloaded open medical models on the Hugging Face Hub.

Vendor and capital tracking comes from KLAS and Rock Health. KLAS collects candid feedback from healthcare professionals, including executives, physicians, nurses, and administrators, and publishes Best in KLAS rankings for healthcare IT software and services companies. Rock Health publishes research on digital health funding, but the excerpt does not state current funding totals. No deployment-level ROI figures appear in these excerpts; the closest cost evidence is the HealthBench cost-performance note above.

On risk and governance, WHO identifies ethical challenges and risks with AI for health and sets out six consensus principles plus recommendations to hold public and private stakeholders accountable. NIH points to policies, guidelines, and best practices for investigators. HealthBench stresses that model reliability is critical because a single unsafe or incorrect answer can outweigh the benefit of many good ones, and that while recent models show improved worst-of-n performance, significant room for further gains remains.

A reader deciding whether to deploy should weigh the measured adoption of 24.7%, the benchmark evidence that frontier models are improving but still have reliability gaps, and the governance expectations from WHO and NIH. Vendor claims should be checked against KLAS provider feedback and Rock Health capital tracking rather than taken at face value.

https://klasresearch.com/.brief: KLAS Research is a community that brings together healthcare leaders, IT professionals, and vendors to share candid provider feedback and collaborate on best practices. The organization gathers insights directly from thousands of healthcare professionals, executives, physicians, nurses, IT staff, and administrators, who use IT solutions and services, and uses that feedback to produce market reports and live data. Its annual Best in KLAS report ranks software and services companies that help healthcare organizations achieve the Quadruple Aim, based on year-long feedback from provider and payer professionals. Since 1996, KLAS has aimed to improve healthcare by amplifying provider and payer voices and expanding its research scope to meet evolving technology needs.

https://artificialanalysis.ai/.brief: Artificial Analysis presents independent comparisons of AI models and API hosting providers across quality, price, output speed, and latency. The page indicates whether model weights are available and flags licenses that restrict commercial use or prohibit it entirely. It describes the AA-AnalystAgent benchmark, which runs each question five times to measure how reliably a model reproduces a correct answer on spreadsheet and document analysis. The site also reports the cost of running its Intelligence Index evaluations using token prices, output speed in tokens per second after the first chunk, and a composite score showing how much accuracy a provider endpoint preserves compared with a self-hosted reference.

https://rockhealth.com/insights/.brief: The page says it publishes perspectives on trends shaping the future of healthcare. It notes that its work is at the forefront of digital health. Readers are invited to browse its research on digital health funding and special topics in the healthcare industry. The research is described as “widely-cited.”

https://openai.com/index/healthbench/.brief: HealthBench is a new benchmark for AI in healthcare that evaluates models in realistic scenarios, built with input from 262 physicians across 60 countries. It contains 5,000 “realistic health conversations,” each graded by a physician-written rubric with 48,562 unique criteria, and responses are scored by a GPT-4.1 grader. OpenAI reports that its frontier models, such as o3, have outperformed others and improved by 28% on HealthBench, while a small GPT-4.1 nano model now outperforms the older GPT-4o at 25× lower cost. The benchmark also includes a “HealthBench Hard” subset of 1,000 difficult examples and tracks worst-of-n reliability curves, showing room for further gains.

https://datascience.nih.gov/artificial-i.brief: NIH reports that it makes a wealth of biomedical data available to research communities. It aims to make these data “findable, accessible, interoperable, and reusable, or FAIR” and usable with AI/ML applications. NIH notes that its unique data types, electronic health records, omics, imaging, disease-specific data, create opportunities for novel AI/ML approaches. The agency also emphasizes establishing partnerships and providing policies, guidelines, and best practices for investigators using AI in biomedical and behavioral research, and references Data Management Frameworks.

https://www.who.int/publications/i/item/.brief: The WHO report on ethics and governance of AI for health outlines the ethical challenges and risks of using AI in healthcare and presents six consensus principles to ensure AI benefits all countries. It was developed over eighteen months by experts in ethics, digital technology, law, human rights, and ministries of health. The guidance stresses that AI technologies, which can improve diagnosis, treatment, research, drug development, and support public health functions such as surveillance and outbreak response, must center ethics and human rights in their design, deployment, and use. It also offers recommendations to hold public and private stakeholders accountable and responsive to healthcare workers and affected communities.

https://theworldofai.org/ai-ecosystem/te.brief: According to the page, it catalogues the 1,000 most-downloaded open medical models on the Hugging Face Hub, showing each model’s licence, download count, and release date, with the list refreshed daily. It says the data is drawn from the Hugging Face Hub public API, sorted by all-time downloads, and every entry links to its own Hub page. The page also states that its full-text search covers other database-built resources, including state AI laws, a lawsuit tracker, a glossary, a tools directory, AI companies, a research library, an MCP server registry, compliance frameworks, sources, people, calculators, and weekly digests. It gives a last-verified date of 2026-09-21.
